newsitem.title: UK: OTC threat must be met before LME revival - traders.
newsitem.headline: OTC threat must be met before LME revival - traders.

text.p: Many in the metals business believe a key battle for the future of the London Metal Exchange (LME) may well be fought in the area of the Over-the-Counter (OTC) market.
These contracts -- dependent on LME prices but otherwise independent and, many claim, unregulated -- are a vital part of the overall global metals market.
Traders say they were a key factor in the unauthorised trading of former Sumitomo Corp star trader Yasuo Hamanaka.
These OTC contracts have often provided the vital guarantee or justification for large bank financing of new metal projects as they have provided a floor price for future output.
Unfortunately, metal buyers have not wanted to make matching forward commitments so banks have had to take the strain, trying to manage this risk in volatile and whiplashed markets.
The LME recognises this in its planned January start-up of traded average rate options (TAPOs), but some brokers still feel these options lack natural liquidity.

"After losing huge amounts granting this type of option, some large banks have withdrawn from this market, as despite what some traders believed, it proved impossible to manage the risk involved in such an unbalanced market," said one senior broker.

"The problem was simple in that while metal producers were natural buyers of such options, there was not a natural seller and this left the banks who sold the options unable to manage their risk in a volatile market," said another senior trader.

This year, talk of reform is not just idle chatter. In the wake of the Sumitomo scandal, Britain's leading financial regulator, the Securities and Investment Board (SIB), is making a detailed analysis of the global metal trade, due by the year-end.

There are many items that will come under discussion this week, when many world metals industry representatives meet for the annual London Metals Week, as all with an interest in non-ferrous metals make final amendments to a detailed questionaire the SIB circulated.
But brokers, bankers and traders agree that at least one more veil will be lifted on the LME, making its trading more transparent, modern and understandable.
Many believe the OTC issue will have to be grasped before the LME can return to the record volumes it was seeing before Sumitomo's $2.6 billion copper losses.
